questions.solution:
Trace the program step by step:

[latex]a=5,\ b=11,\ c=20[/latex].
[latex]\text{ptr}=\&a[/latex] (ptr now points to [latex]a[/latex]).
[latex]{*}\text{ptr}=c[/latex] → sets [latex]a=20[/latex] (since ptr points to [latex]a[/latex], and we assign it [latex]c[/latex]'s current value [latex]20[/latex]).
[latex]\text{ptr}=\&c[/latex] (ptr now points to [latex]c[/latex] instead).
[latex]a={*}(\&b)[/latex] → sets [latex]a=b=11[/latex] (overwriting the earlier [latex]20[/latex]).
[latex]c={*}\text{ptr}-a[/latex] → [latex]{*}\text{ptr}[/latex] is [latex]c[/latex] itself (since ptr points to [latex]c[/latex]), whose value is still [latex]20[/latex] (unchanged since it was first set); so [latex]c=20-a=20-11=9[/latex].

[latex]\text{printf}[/latex] prints the final value of [latex]c[/latex], which is [latex]9[/latex].

Answer: 9

[latex]\text{arr}=\{30,50,10,0,0\}[/latex] (remaining elements zero-initialized, since at least one initializer was given).

[latex]\text{ptr}=\&\text{arr[0]}+1[/latex] → points to [latex]\text{arr[1]}=50[/latex].
[latex]a={*}\text{ptr}[/latex] → [latex]a=50[/latex].
[latex]({*}\text{ptr})++[/latex] → increments [latex]\text{arr[1]}[/latex] from [latex]50[/latex] to [latex]51[/latex].
[latex]\text{ptr}++[/latex] → now points to [latex]\text{arr[2]}=10[/latex] (unaffected).

[latex]\text{printf}[/latex] computes [latex]a+({*}\text{ptr})+\text{arr[1]}=50+10+51=111[/latex] (using [latex]\text{arr[1]}[/latex]'s updated value [latex]51[/latex], since the increment already happened).

Answer: 111

[latex]a="@\#Hello\ World!"[/latex] occupies indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]14[/latex] (`@`,`#`,`H`,`e`,`l`,`l`,`o`,` `,`W`,`o`,`r`,`l`,`d`,`!`,`\0`). [latex]\text{stringcopy(a, a+2)}[/latex] sets [latex]s=a[/latex] (index [latex]0[/latex]) and [latex]t=a+2[/latex] (index [latex]2[/latex]), copying forward while [latex]{*}t[/latex] is non-null (checked before each copy).

Since the loop condition is checked before copying, it copies indices [latex]2[/latex] through [latex]13[/latex] (`H` through `!`, [latex]12[/latex] characters) into destination indices [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]11[/latex], then stops as soon as [latex]{*}t[/latex] hits the original null at index [latex]14[/latex] — without ever writing a new null terminator into the destination.

So after the copy: indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]11[/latex] hold the shifted text `Hello World!`, but indices [latex]12,13,14[/latex] still hold their original, untouched values: `d`, `!`, and the original `\0`.

[latex]\text{printf("\%s")}[/latex] prints from index [latex]0[/latex] until it hits the first null — which is still the original one at index [latex]14[/latex]. So it prints: `Hello World!` (indices 0-11) followed by the leftover `d` (index 12) and `!` (index 13) before finally stopping at the null.

Answer: Hello World!d!

questions.text:
#include <stdio.h>
void foo(int *p, int x) {
    *p = x;
}

int main() {
    int *z;
    int a = 20, b = 25;
    z = &a;
    foo(z, b);
    printf("%d", a);
    return 0;
}
The output of the given C program is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.solution:
[latex]\text{z}=\&\text{a}[/latex] makes [latex]z[/latex] point to [latex]a[/latex] (currently [latex]20[/latex]).

[latex]\text{foo(z, b)}[/latex] passes [latex]z[/latex] (the address of [latex]a[/latex]) and [latex]b[/latex]'s value ([latex]25[/latex]) into [latex]\text{foo(int *p, int x)}[/latex], so inside [latex]\text{foo}[/latex], [latex]p[/latex] points to [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]x=25[/latex].

[latex]{*}\text{p}=\text{x}[/latex] writes [latex]25[/latex] into whatever [latex]p[/latex] points to — i.e. directly into [latex]a[/latex] itself (since pointers give real access to the caller's variable). So [latex]a[/latex] becomes [latex]25[/latex].

[latex]\text{printf}[/latex] then prints the now-updated [latex]a[/latex].

Answer: 25

questions.text:
The pseudocode of a function fun() is given below: 

fun(int A[0,...,n-1])
{
    for i=0 to n-2
	for j=0 to n-i-2
	    if (A[j] > A[j+1])
		then swap A[j] and A[j+1]
}
Let [latex]A[0, \dots, 29][/latex] be an array storing 30 distinct integers in descending order. The number of swap operations that will be performed, if the function fun() is called with [latex]A[0, \dots, 29][/latex] as argument, is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.solution:
This is exactly the standard bubble-sort pseudocode. On a fully descending-order array, every single adjacent-pair comparison across the entire double loop finds the pair out of order, so a swap happens on every comparison — there are no comparisons at all that skip the swap.

Total comparisons (and hence swaps) [latex]=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i)=\binom{n}{2}[/latex] for an [latex]n[/latex]-element array. With [latex]n=30[/latex]: [latex]\binom{30}{2}=\dfrac{30\times29}{2}=435[/latex].

Answer: 435
